newsitem.title: FRANCE: French government in quandary on Superphenix plant.
newsitem.headline: French government in quandary on Superphenix plant.

text.p: France's Environment Minister clashed with a fellow cabinet member on Tuesday over whether to restart the 60 billion franc ($10.5 billion) Superphenix fast-breeder reactor which has been plagued by faults since it was built 20 years ago.

The dispute pits Corinne Lepage, who wants the now-idle 1,200 megawatt plant to stay shut until a new inquiry determines its fate, against Industry Minister Franck Borotra, who wants to restart it immediately.
The Council of State last week cancelled a decree dating from July 1994 authorising the restarting of the reactor in Creys Malville in the Alps, which had been operating as a research reactor.

After an appeal from environmentalists, who call the reactor a dangerous and costly dinosaur, the Council ruled that the procedure for transforming the plant into a research prototype was flawed and required a new public inquiry.

The Council said the decree and an initial inquiry had been based on the idea that Superphenix would be used to produce electricity, although the nuclear safety board decided three years ago it would only be viable as a research tool.
Borotra, backed by the nuclear lobby, wants simply to change the 1994 decree to allow Superphenix, which has operated for less than a year of its existence, to restart without delay.

"I am asking that there be a new open public inquiry on Superphenix as a research tool. It's not by hiding problems that we solve them," Lepage told the daily Le Monde in an interview published on Tuesday.
Satirical weekly Le Canard Enchaine said Lepage had threatened to resign if Superphenix was restarted without a probe. Her office declined to comment on the report.
Officials at Prime Minister Alain Juppe's office said the government wanted to keep Superphenix operating, but had not yet decided if it would modify the decree or launch a new inquiry.
"The government has decided to continue Superphenix's activity. The necessary measures will be taken in the next few days," an official said.
Borotra and Lepage are also locking horns over the choice of a new head of France's nuclear safety agency, the IPSN.

Lepage, due to meet Prime Minister Alain Juppe on Tuesday to discuss both issues, has opposed Borotra's choice of Dominique Maillard, a senior executive of the SNCF state railway, whom she feels is too closely linked to the nuclear lobby.

"It's not the first time I've come up against the nuclear lobby, it's inevitable for an environment minister," Lepage said. "The fight is unequal because I'm confronted by people who have enormous means."
Lepage is pushing for her own candidate, Renaud Abord de Chatillon, one of her close aides.

Eighty members of the IPSN have signed a petition against Maillard's appointment, saying he is a stooge of the nuclear industry. IPSN officials would like to see a third person, Daniel Queniart, currently head of nuclear safety at the agency, get the job.
